chapter_theme: A single song at Kannapuram (கன்னபுரம்) on the Kaveri, against the sects: the poet asks to be rid of the pettiness of 'this is mine', of learning the books of yoga and other paths, and to be given a life that cannot be called 'this'; the praise shows Murugan waiting outside Valli's cave at night like a thief.

811.reading: The poet speaks of thinking that this flesh body made of food, under the reckoning of Brahma born on the lotus, will not die, of entering others' paths and learning the many books of the delusion called yoga, and of the pettiness of sect that says 'this is for me'; he asks whether Murugan will not destroy that pettiness, free him from trouble and give a life that cannot be named 'this'. The praise shows Murugan, for the girl with cane-sweet speech, braided hair and swan's gait, standing sweating late at night at the mouth of a cave in the hill like a burglar, unable to enter; it names the Lord of Kannapuram on the Ponni with the serpent bracelet and Murugan lord of the kings of the golden world.
811.nuance: The song alliterates on அன்ன/இன்ன/கன்ன throughout, so word division is uncertain. இன்னது எனக்கு என்னும் மதப் புன்மை: the fault named is sectarian pride; முச்சடங்க யோகம் may refer to a threefold practice. இன்னது எனப்படா வாழ்க்கை: the life asked for cannot be named or defined. கன்னமிட in the praise compares Murugan at Valli's cave to a housebreaker, a striking image.
